sourceRefs.citation: Geneve RL, Janes EW, Kester ST, Hildebrand DF, Davis D. Temperature Limits for Seed Germination in Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.). Crops. 2022;2(4):415-427.
sourceRefs.supports: Seed germination rate is temperature-dependent and should be evaluated with cultivar and test conditions in mind rather than treated as a fixed calendar event.

sourceRefs.citation: Caplan D, Stemeroff J, Dixon M, Zheng Y. Vegetative propagation of cannabis by stem cuttings: effects of leaf number, cutting position, rooting hormone, and leaf tip removal. Can J Plant Sci. 2018;98(5):1126-1132.
sourceRefs.supports: Cannabis cutting propagation success depends on propagation choices; rooting quality and success are measurable outcomes rather than assumptions based on leaf appearance.

sourceRefs.citation: Richards CD, Ryu B-R, Gim G-J, Park S-H. Hermaphroditism in Cannabis sativa L.: Impacts, Inducers, and Industry Implications. Plants. 2026;15(11):1643.
sourceRefs.supports: Cannabis sex expression is plastic and context-dependent; genotype, developmental stage, hormones, treatments and environment can interact, so one stress event does not prove a single cause of intersexual expression.

sourceRefs.citation: Nimmala M, Ross SD, Foroutan H. Cannabis pollen dispersal across the United States. Sci Rep. 2024;14:20605.
sourceRefs.supports: Cannabis pollen is windborne and dispersal depends on meteorological context; a fixed universal isolation distance cannot guarantee zero pollen exposure.

sourceRefs.citation: Kay ER, Philbin CS, Richards LA, Forister ML, Jeffrey C, Dyer LA. Effects of Water and Wind Stress on Phytochemical Diversity, Cannabinoid Composition, and Arthropod Diversity in Hemp. Plants. 2025;14(3):474; corrected 2026.
sourceRefs.supports: Outdoor hemp responses can shift after water deficit, flooding and wind stress, and cultivar effects can be large; weather exposure should be recorded as context rather than inferred from symptoms alone.

sourceRefs.citation: Baek Y, Grab H, Chen C. Postharvest Drying and Curing Affect Cannabinoid Contents and Microbial Levels in Industrial Hemp (Cannabis sativa L.). Plants. 2025;14(3):414.
sourceRefs.supports: Drying and curing conditions alter moisture, decarboxylation, color and microbial levels; postharvest quality problems require measured process and storage evidence.

cases.title: A seed lot is germinating slowly and unevenly
cases.presenting: A tray from one seed lot shows delayed and uneven radicle emergence. The grower assumes the lot is dead and wants to change several inputs at once.
evidence: The same lot shows a broad spread in time-to-germination rather than a single synchronized event.
Seed-zone temperature is lower than the room sensor suggests and varies across the tray.
The medium is moist and aerated rather than waterlogged, and there is no strong decay odor.
A comparison lot in the same setup germinates faster, so both lot effects and temperature remain plausible.

differential.reason: Measured seed-zone temperature is below the faster range for the comparison and is spatially uneven.
The comparison lot performs better, so lot vigor may also contribute and should be tested rather than assumed.
External fertilizer is not the primary driver of the earliest germination event and does not explain the temperature pattern.

cases.interpretation: The best working interpretation is a temperature-and-lot interaction, not proof that the entire lot is nonviable.
cases.why: Germination is a time-to-event process. A single final check can hide differences in rate and vigor, and room temperature is not necessarily seed-zone temperature.
cases.action: Stabilize the seed-zone environment and continue a defined germination test without adding unrelated treatments. Keep the lot identity intact.
cases.verify: Record new radicle emergence by time. If the final normal-seedling percentage remains poor under controlled conditions, then low lot vigor or viability gains weight.

cases.title: Seedlings emerge, then several collapse at the media line
cases.presenting: Several recently emerged seedlings develop a pinched or weak stem near the media surface and fall over. The tray has stayed persistently wet.
evidence: Losses occur after emergence rather than before radicle protrusion.
The affected cells remain wetter than healthy comparison cells and have limited air-filled porosity.
Failure is clustered rather than evenly distributed across the entire seed lot.
No single pathogen has been laboratory-confirmed from the collapsed tissue.

differential.reason: Persistent wetness and post-emergence collapse support a root-collar disease or low-oxygen environment, but species-level confirmation is absent.
The seeds completed germination and emergence, so the failure gate is later than basic seed viability.
A nutrient shortage is not the best explanation for abrupt clustered collapse at the media line.

cases.interpretation: A wet seedling-zone failure is strongly supported, with damping-off or secondary pathogen involvement possible but not proven to species.
cases.why: The key evidence is when failure occurs and where it is located. 'Seed did not make it' is too broad to diagnose the failure stage.
cases.action: Separate affected cells, correct avoidable saturation and sanitation problems, and preserve representative samples if pathogen confirmation is important.
cases.verify: Track incidence among newly emerged seedlings and compare moisture/aeration conditions between affected and unaffected cells.

cases.title: Cuttings stay green but are not rooting
cases.presenting: A clone tray still looks mostly green after the expected internal schedule, but destructive checks show little root initiation and the grower wants to increase fertilizer.
evidence: Several cuttings remain turgid enough to look alive but have weak or absent roots.
The tray record shows inconsistent donor-leaf preparation and propagation treatment between batches.
Rooting media temperature and moisture have not been logged at the cutting base.
A previous batch from the same donor rooted normally under a different propagation setup.

differential.reason: Rooting outcomes can change with cutting preparation and rooting treatment, and this batch differs from the successful reference.
The same donor previously rooted, so a fixed genetic inability is poorly supported.
Green leaves without roots do not show that more nutrient concentration will solve adventitious root initiation.

cases.interpretation: The propagation process is the best-supported investigation target; a green cutting is not the same as a rooted cutting.
cases.why: Rooting success and root quality are distinct measurable outcomes. Visual survival above the media can delay recognition of failed root initiation.
cases.action: Standardize cutting preparation and propagation conditions, then compare a controlled batch rather than stacking new inputs onto the current tray.
cases.verify: Use destructive sample checks or another defined root-quality measure at scheduled intervals and compare success by batch.

cases.title: Freshly rooted clones stall after transplant
cases.presenting: Clones with visible roots are transplanted and then show several days of poor extension growth and intermittent droop. The grower calls it a nutrient deficiency immediately.
evidence: Roots were visible at transplant but root volume differed substantially among clones.
The new container holds more water than the propagation plug and the irrigation routine was not adjusted.
Symptoms are strongest on the least-rooted transplants.
There is no new pest evidence and no documented nutrient-mixing error.

differential.reason: Root-system size and a changed water environment align with the plants that are stalling.
Possible if the new root zone is limiting uptake, but there is no direct evidence of a missing element.
No propagation-network pattern or supporting direct evidence has appeared yet.

cases.interpretation: Transplant establishment and root-zone water balance are the leading explanation, not a confirmed elemental deficiency.
cases.why: A rooted cutting still has to establish a larger functional root system after transplant, and irrigation behavior changes when container volume and media geometry change.
cases.action: Stabilize irrigation around the actual root-zone condition and avoid changing multiple nutrient variables simultaneously.
cases.verify: Compare new extension growth, leaf posture and root-zone moisture against better-rooted transplants over the same interval.

cases.title: Two pH readings disagree on the same irrigation event
cases.presenting: A grower records one pH value from the source solution and a very different value from runoff, then concludes the medium has an exact 'lockout pH' from those two numbers.
evidence: The two samples came from different locations and represent different material.
The meters were not checked against fresh calibration standards before the comparison.
Runoff volume and timing varied between containers.
Plant symptoms are not uniform across plants despite the claimed single pH cause.

differential.reason: Different samples and uncontrolled collection methods can legitimately produce different values before biology is invoked.
Possible, but it needs a repeatable root-zone sampling method and calibrated instrumentation to characterize.

differential.cause: Guaranteed nutrient lockout at one pH number
differential.reason: A single reading does not prove a universal lockout threshold or identify which nutrient is limiting.

cases.interpretation: The first problem is measurement comparability. The data do not yet support an exact root-zone diagnosis.
cases.why: Accuracy, precision, sample identity and method belong in the diagnosis. Numbers without method metadata can look more certain than they are.
cases.action: Calibrate instruments, define where and how each sample is collected, repeat the measurement, and compare with plant and root-zone evidence.
cases.verify: If repeatable same-method measurements continue to diverge in a consistent direction, then investigate the root-zone chemistry mechanism.

cases.title: EC is rising while growth slows and leaves droop
cases.presenting: A container crop shows slowing growth, intermittent droop and a rising root-zone EC trend. The grower proposes adding more fertilizer because lower leaves are pale.
evidence: EC has increased across repeated same-method measurements rather than from one sample.
Container dryback has become more extreme while feed concentration stayed similar.
Drainage and irrigation timing changed shortly before the trend began.
No analytical evidence shows that the total nutrient solution is deficient in concentration.

differential.reason: Rising EC plus stronger dryback and changed irrigation provide a coherent root-zone mechanism.
Specific deficiency can coexist, but adding total concentration is not justified by the EC evidence.
It does not explain the measured root-zone trend and whole-plant slowing.

cases.interpretation: Root-zone concentration and water balance deserve priority over increasing total fertilizer strength.
cases.why: EC reports ionic concentration, not the identity of every nutrient, and high concentration does not imply that more fertilizer is beneficial.
cases.action: Correct the irrigation/process driver and return the root zone toward the intended program without making unrelated changes.
cases.verify: Follow same-method EC, substrate water status, new growth and plant posture to see whether the trend reverses.

cases.title: Sticky leaves and curled tips are being called a deficiency
cases.presenting: Young leaves are curled and some surfaces feel sticky. The grower focuses on nutrient charts because the insects are small and clustered under tender growth.
evidence: Magnified inspection finds aphid colonies on shoots and leaf undersides.
Cast skins and sticky honeydew occur in the same zones as the colonies.
The distribution is patchy and expands between scouting dates.
Neighboring unaffected plants receive the same nutrient solution.

differential.reason: Live colonies, cast skins and honeydew are direct organism evidence.
The common feed does not explain localized colonies and honeydew.
Powdery mildew does not produce aphid bodies, cast skins or honeydew.

cases.interpretation: Aphid pressure is confirmed in the sampled zones.
cases.why: Direct organism evidence outranks a look-alike leaf curl pattern.
cases.action: Map colonies, inspect neighboring plants and apply a lawful IPM response appropriate to crop stage and the confirmed pest.
cases.verify: Repeat counts on the same shoots or leaves and track whether colony expansion slows or reverses.

cases.title: Unexpected seeds appear in an intended unseeded flower crop
cases.presenting: A previously unseeded flowering room begins producing scattered seeds. No intentionally flowering male plant is present in the room.
evidence: Mature or developing seeds are confirmed inside pistillate flowers.
A detailed flower inspection finds a small number of anthers on some otherwise female inflorescences.
Outdoor or neighboring pollen exposure cannot be ruled out from the current records.
The event is not uniform across every plant or every room zone.

differential.cause: Intersexual flower expression with self/nearby pollination
differential.reason: Observed anthers provide a plausible local pollen source and cannabis sex expression can be plastic.
Cannabis pollen can disperse with wind, so outside exposure remains plausible without stronger containment evidence.
Nutrient stress can affect plant health but does not itself replace the requirement for pollination and fertilization to form normal seeds.

cases.interpretation: Pollination is confirmed by seed set, but the pollen source is not yet fully resolved.
cases.why: Finding anthers changes the source ranking, yet it does not prove every seed came from that source; airflow, timing and genetic identity matter.
cases.action: Map seeded flowers and any anthers, preserve plant identity, review airflow/contact history and separate suspect reproductive material.
cases.verify: Trace seed distribution and pollen-source evidence over time; genetic testing can be used if parentage matters enough to justify it.

cases.title: Outdoor plants are damaged after an extreme wind event
cases.presenting: After a strong wind event, several outdoor plants show torn leaves, bent stems and a temporary growth slowdown. New spots appearing later are being assumed to be the same injury.
evidence: Mechanical tears and stem damage align with the documented wind event.
Damage is strongest on exposed edges rather than uniformly through sheltered plants.
Some later lesions do not share the same shape or location as the original mechanical injury.
Weather exposure and plant position are available in the field record.

differential.reason: Timing, exposed-edge distribution and physical injury support wind damage for the initial symptoms.
Later lesions with a different pattern should be evaluated separately rather than automatically attributed to wind.
A nutrient shortage is less consistent with exposure-edge mechanical damage after a known event.

cases.interpretation: The original injury is best explained by wind, but later symptoms should be treated as a new diagnostic question if their pattern differs.
cases.why: Outdoor crops can experience multiple sequential stresses. One known event should not become a permanent explanation for every symptom afterward.
cases.action: Stabilize damaged plants as appropriate, document the affected zones and start a separate scouting record for any newly developing lesion pattern.
cases.verify: Compare recovery of new growth and the incidence of new lesions in exposed versus sheltered zones.

cases.title: Plants droop after repeated heavy rain
cases.presenting: Outdoor container plants droop and pale after several days of heavy rain. The grower wants to feed immediately because the foliage looks hungry.
evidence: Containers remain much heavier than their normal irrigation baseline.
Drainage is slow and root-zone aeration is likely reduced.
Symptoms appear after the rain sequence across the wettest containers first.
There is no documented feed-mixing change immediately before the event.

differential.reason: The water history, container weight and spatial pattern strongly support saturation.

differential.cause: Nutrient uptake limitation secondary to root stress
differential.reason: Uptake can be affected by a stressed root zone, but adding more concentration does not address the primary water condition.
The timing is tied more closely to the rain/saturation event than to a change in nutrient supply.

cases.interpretation: Saturation/root-zone stress is the leading explanation, with secondary nutrient symptoms possible.
cases.why: Water and nutrient symptoms interact. Treating the leaf color alone can worsen a root-zone problem if concentration is increased before aeration recovers.
cases.action: Restore drainage and allow the root zone to move back toward its normal water/air balance before making large nutrient changes.
cases.verify: Track container weight or moisture, root condition and new growth as the weather clears.

cases.title: Drying flower develops a musty odor and uneven moisture
cases.presenting: During drying, outer flower surfaces feel dry while denser interiors remain moist and a musty odor appears in part of the batch.
evidence: Moisture is visibly and tactilely nonuniform across flower density and position.
The problem is strongest in dense material with slower air exchange.
A musty odor appears during a period of prolonged moisture retention.
No validated microbial result has yet identified a specific organism or toxin.

differential.cause: Uneven drying with elevated microbial-spoilage risk
differential.reason: Persistent interior moisture and odor during drying support a process-control and microbial-risk problem.
An unexplained musty odor plus wet interiors should not be normalized as desirable curing.
Maturity can affect chemistry and structure but does not explain the measured/observed moisture nonuniformity by itself.

cases.interpretation: Uneven drying with microbial-spoilage risk is strongly supported; species or toxin claims require testing.
cases.why: Postharvest safety cannot be judged from outer crispness alone. Dense interiors can retain water after surfaces feel dry.
cases.action: Segregate suspect material, verify the drying environment and moisture/water-activity process, and follow applicable quality and testing procedures before release.
cases.verify: Use repeatable moisture or water-activity measurements and batch inspection to confirm the process is converging uniformly.

cases.title: A dried batch becomes brittle and loses aroma rapidly
cases.presenting: One dried batch becomes unusually brittle and its aroma drops quickly compared with a reference batch of the same cultivar.
evidence: The affected batch experienced a faster, warmer drying profile than the reference batch.
Drying endpoint was judged only by feel and no batch moisture or water-activity record was kept.
The reference batch retained more pliability and aroma under a slower documented process.
There is no evidence that the two batches differed in genetics.

differential.reason: The process difference aligns with faster moisture removal and lower aroma retention.
The batches share cultivar identity and the major known difference is postharvest process.

differential.cause: Guaranteed proof of low cannabinoid content
differential.reason: Brittleness or aroma alone does not quantify cannabinoid concentration.

cases.interpretation: The postharvest process is the best-supported cause of the quality difference, but chemical potency cannot be inferred from feel or smell alone.
cases.why: Drying changes water, volatile compounds and chemistry in cultivar- and process-dependent ways; sensory observations are useful but incomplete measurements.
cases.action: Standardize and record the drying process, then compare future batches with objective endpoint measurements appropriate to the operation.
cases.verify: Compare moisture/water activity, aroma retention and—when needed—laboratory chemistry across matched batches.

nodes.question: Is the failure before radicle protrusion?
nodes.yes: Check seed condition, time-to-event, seed-zone temperature, moisture and oxygen.
nodes.no: If radicles emerged, move to emergence/establishment rather than seed viability.

nodes.question: Is seed-zone temperature measured at the seed and stable?
nodes.yes: Compare it with the tested range for the cultivar or a valid reference lot.
nodes.no: Measure the seed zone; do not substitute room air temperature.

nodes.question: Is the medium moist but still aerated?
nodes.yes: Keep moisture method consistent and compare lots.
nodes.no: Correct saturation or repeated drying before blaming genetics.

nodes.question: Does a comparison lot perform normally in the same setup?
nodes.yes: Lot vigor/viability gains weight.
nodes.no: Environment or method remains a stronger common cause.

nodes.question: Does the lot still underperform after controlled retest?
nodes.yes: Document the lot as low-performing under the test and investigate vigor/viability.
nodes.no: Continue establishment tracking; do not call delayed seeds dead prematurely.

decisionTrees.title: A clone tray is not rooting

nodes.question: Have roots been measured rather than inferred from green leaves?
nodes.yes: Score rooting success/root quality on a defined sample.
nodes.no: Create a root check; shoot survival alone is not the endpoint.

nodes.question: Were donor identity and cutting preparation consistent?
nodes.yes: Compare rooting environment and treatment variables next.
nodes.no: Standardize donor/cutting preparation before comparing batches.

nodes.question: Were basal-zone moisture and temperature recorded?
nodes.yes: Compare failed and successful batches using the same method.
nodes.no: Instrument the propagation zone before adding inputs.

nodes.question: Did the same donor root successfully in a prior controlled batch?
nodes.yes: Process/environment gains weight over fixed donor inability.
nodes.no: Donor health or identity deserves more scrutiny.

nodes.question: Does a controlled repeat improve rooting?
nodes.yes: Keep the standardized protocol and record batch outcomes.
nodes.no: Escalate to donor health, pathogen testing or additional propagation variables.

decisionTrees.title: pH or EC numbers do not agree

nodes.question: Are the values from the same sample type and location?
nodes.yes: Check instrument and timing comparability.
nodes.no: Do not compare source, drain, runoff and media extracts as if they are identical samples.

nodes.question: Was the instrument checked with appropriate standards?
nodes.yes: Repeat the sample with method metadata.
nodes.no: Calibrate or verify before interpreting the crop.

nodes.question: Was collection timing/volume consistent?
nodes.yes: Compare repeated same-method trends.
nodes.no: Standardize sampling before calling the difference biological.

nodes.question: Does the repeatable trend match plant/root-zone evidence?
nodes.yes: Investigate the relevant chemical or irrigation mechanism.
nodes.no: Keep alternative explanations open.

nodes.question: Would a proposed correction change several variables at once?
nodes.yes: Use the smallest justified adjustment and remeasure.
nodes.no: Preserve one-variable learning when practical.

decisionTrees.title: Unexpected seed set or male structures appear

nodes.question: Are actual seeds or male floral structures confirmed?
nodes.yes: Map their location and developmental stage.
nodes.no: Do not infer pollination from swollen tissue alone.

nodes.question: Are anthers/male flowers present on otherwise female plants?
nodes.yes: Intersexual expression becomes a local pollen-source candidate.
nodes.no: External or hidden pollen sources remain important.

nodes.question: Could outside or neighboring pollen exposure occur?
nodes.yes: Review airflow, flowering timing and containment history.
nodes.no: Local sources and handling pathways gain weight.

nodes.question: Is the pattern concentrated in one genotype or stress history?
nodes.yes: Genotype/context interaction deserves investigation.
nodes.no: A shared environmental or external pollen source may be more likely.

nodes.question: Does parentage matter for breeding decisions?
nodes.yes: Use traceability and genetic testing if justified.
nodes.no: Manage the crop based on confirmed seed/pollen evidence without inventing parentage.

decisionTrees.title: Outdoor symptoms appear after severe weather

nodes.question: Is there a documented wind, flood, drought or rain event?
nodes.yes: Map symptoms against exposure and timing.
nodes.no: Treat weather as one hypothesis, not a default.

nodes.question: Are injuries mechanical and strongest on exposed edges?
nodes.yes: Wind/mechanical stress gains weight.
nodes.no: Inspect roots, pests, disease lesions and irrigation.

nodes.question: Is the root zone still saturated or unusually dry?
nodes.yes: Prioritize water/oxygen balance evidence.
nodes.no: Move to tissue-specific pest/disease inspection.

nodes.question: Are new lesions different from the original weather injury?
nodes.yes: Open a new differential for secondary disease/pest issues.
nodes.no: Continue recovery tracking.

nodes.question: Does sheltered comparison growth recover differently?
nodes.yes: Use the contrast to test the weather hypothesis.
nodes.no: Reopen systemic causes if exposure does not explain the pattern.

decisionTrees.title: Drying or curing quality is going wrong

nodes.question: Is moisture uniform through dense and thin material?
nodes.yes: Check objective endpoint/process records.
nodes.no: Treat nonuniformity as a process problem before calling it curing.

nodes.question: Is there musty odor, visible growth or other spoilage evidence?
nodes.yes: Segregate suspect material and use appropriate quality/testing procedures.
nodes.no: Continue chemistry and texture evaluation.

nodes.question: Was drying temperature/RH/airflow recorded?
nodes.yes: Compare with a successful batch.
nodes.no: Instrument the process before changing many variables.

nodes.question: Did the batch dry much faster or warmer than the reference?
nodes.yes: Over-aggressive drying/volatile loss gains weight.
nodes.no: Storage and starting-material differences remain plausible.

nodes.question: Are potency or microbial claims being made from smell/feel alone?
nodes.yes: Use laboratory testing when the claim requires it.
nodes.no: Use sensory data as one observation, not the final measurement.
